concepts.decision: Frame continuity around essential outcomes, people, facilities, suppliers, data, and communications—not only IT recovery.
concepts.definition: The organization’s ability and planning discipline to sustain prioritized business functions through disruption and transition to normal operations.
concepts.failureExample: Restoring servers while customer support and approvals cannot operate is not business continuity.
concepts.label: Business Continuity

concepts.decision: Plan with business, facilities, HR, suppliers, and technology owners before an event; revise when their assumptions change.
concepts.definition: The owner-led process of identifying disruption scenarios, priorities, resources, alternatives, roles, and recovery/return criteria.
concepts.failureExample: A technology-only plan may omit staff shortages or contractual dependencies that halt the function.
concepts.label: Continuity Planning

concepts.decision: Have the business owner identify the function and consequence; do not infer criticality from system cost or popularity.
concepts.definition: A business activity whose unacceptable interruption drives a continuity priority, such as payments, safety response, or regulatory reporting.
concepts.failureExample: Treating a high-cost but deferrable system as first priority can delay a time-sensitive obligation.
concepts.label: Critical Function

concepts.decision: Use business-owner input to determine impacts, tolerances, dependencies, and priority; validate when business conditions change.
concepts.definition: A structured assessment of disruption consequences over time that supplies business requirements for continuity and recovery.
concepts.failureExample: An asset inventory cannot reveal the mounting legal or safety consequence of a delayed business process.
concepts.label: Business Impact Analysis

concepts.decision: Set priority through accountable business decisions informed by BIA, then communicate the tradeoff to resource owners.
concepts.definition: The agreed order in which business functions receive continuity resources based on time-sensitive impact and accepted tolerances.
concepts.failureExample: Letting the loudest technical owner choose priority can starve a more time-critical function.
concepts.label: Continuity Priority

concepts.decision: Use when it can safely sustain the function for a defined period; test staffing, records, approvals, and later reconciliation.
concepts.definition: A predesigned nonstandard way to perform a critical function when normal people, place, process, or technology is unavailable.
concepts.failureExample: Paper orders without later reconciliation can preserve availability while corrupting records.
concepts.label: Manual Workaround

concepts.decision: Choose an exercise that tests the business function and its dependencies, not merely technical failover.
concepts.definition: A planned practice of continuity roles, alternatives, and decisions under a disruption scenario.
concepts.failureExample: A server-failover test that never involves business staff leaves continuity of the customer process unknown.
concepts.label: Continuity Exercise

concepts.decision: Include the business function’s real dependencies and explicit exclusions so evidence can be interpreted honestly.
concepts.definition: The stated functions, locations, participants, dependencies, scenario, boundaries, and evidence included in a continuity exercise.
concepts.failureExample: Excluding the verification vendor from a payment continuity exercise produces a misleading pass.
concepts.label: Exercise Scope

concepts.decision: Collect outcomes such as timelines, work products, decision records, reconciliation, and owner acceptance against stated criteria.
concepts.definition: Objective records showing whether the prioritized function, communication, alternative process, and acceptance conditions performed as planned.
concepts.failureExample: Attendance and enthusiastic discussion do not prove the function continued within its tolerance.
concepts.label: Continuity Evidence

concepts.decision: Predefine audience, authority, channels, and the difference between exercise status and real-event notices.
concepts.definition: Internal and external messages that coordinate roles, affected customers, suppliers, leadership, and transition decisions during disruption.
concepts.failureExample: Conflicting customer messages can compound disruption even when operations are recovering.
concepts.label: Continuity Communications

concepts.decision: Prioritize by effect on the critical function, route changes through governance, and retest the altered capability.
concepts.definition: An owned corrective change that removes or reduces a tested continuity gap and is verified after implementation.
concepts.failureExample: Closing a vendor-dependency finding without testing the alternate supplier leaves the continuity gap open.
concepts.label: Continuity Remediation

concepts.decision: Identify dependency owners, agreements, alternate options, contact paths, and failure assumptions in the plan and exercise.
concepts.definition: A supplier, utility, service, regulator, or other outside party whose availability or decision affects continuity of a function.
concepts.failureExample: A continuity plan that assumes a cloud, telecom, or verification vendor is always available fails under shared disruption.
concepts.label: External Dependency

misconceptions.claim: Continuity is the IT department's recovery plan.
misconceptions.correction: Business owners, people, facilities, suppliers, communications, security, and technology all contribute to continuity.

misconceptions.claim: A documented alternate site proves continuity.
misconceptions.correction: People, data, identity, suppliers, communications, workarounds, and acceptance must be exercised as well.

outcome: Given a business disruption, identify critical functions and dependencies, select continuity workarounds or recovery priorities, exercise the plan, and capture improvements that protect the mission rather than only the technology.

sections.body: Business continuity planning identifies critical functions, impacts, priorities, tolerances, resources, dependencies, and acceptable workarounds. A business impact analysis helps owners describe consequences over time, while security and technology teams translate those needs into service, data, identity, facility, supplier, and recovery requirements. Choose priority and recovery assumptions with the business owner; do not derive them from a technology inventory alone. Continuity is broader than disaster recovery because it includes manual operations, staffing, alternate communications, customers, and external dependencies.
keyPoints: Business owners define mission priority and impact; technical teams help make the requirement executable.
Dependencies include people, suppliers, data, facilities, identity, communications, and regulatory obligations.
A workaround can preserve a function while a technical recovery proceeds, but it needs authorization, safety, data, and evidence controls.
sections.title: Plan continuity around functions and dependencies

sections.body: Continuity exercises test decisions, communications, roles, workarounds, supplier coordination, and transition criteria. Define scope, objective, observers, evidence, communications, and stop criteria; use injects that reflect missing people, limited facilities, delayed vendors, degraded data, or public communication pressure. Record what participants assumed, what worked, what failed, and which owner will change the plan, contract, training, technology, or priority. A corrective action is complete only when the changed continuity capability is accepted and retested.
keyPoints: A continuity exercise should test business decisions and dependencies, not only system failover.
Exercise communications should distinguish a test from a real event and protect sensitive plans.
Corrective actions should be prioritized, owned, evidenced, and retested.
sections.title: Exercise continuity, communicate, and improve

summary: Business continuity keeps prioritized business functions operating through disruption by aligning people, processes, technology, facilities, suppliers, communications, and recovery priorities.

assumptions: The scenario is a bounded application of the canonical unit, not a universal threshold, legal conclusion, or vendor prescription.
Directed edges carry only their printed relation; proximity and shared color do not imply ownership, authorization, or chronology.
Acceptance applies only to the stated scope and retained evidence; unknown or excluded conditions remain explicit.
